I study how trees respond to climate extremes — heatwaves, drought, and the
shifting baselines of a warming world — and what those responses tell us about
resilience, recovery, and mortality. My work combines **ecological and climate
time-series analysis**, **statistical and machine-learning models**, and
**dynamical-systems thinking**, drawing on dendrometer records, flux-tower data,
global tree-ring archives, and high-resolution climate datasets.

Across projects, a single question recurs: *how do short-term climate extremes
reshape the long-term trajectory of tree growth, function, and survival?* I
approach it from several directions at once — data-driven, mechanistic, and
instrumental — because the answer lives at the intersection of all three.

---

## Disentangling soil and atmospheric drought

*How trees grow, shrink, and recover under two different kinds of drought.*

Drought is not one thing. Trees experience it both through the **soil** (falling
water availability at the roots) and through the **atmosphere** (rising vapor
pressure deficit that pulls water from the canopy). These two pressures often
arrive together, which makes their individual effects hard to separate — yet they
act on the tree through different mechanisms.

Using high-resolution **dendrometer** time series, I disentangle how soil versus
atmospheric drought drive the daily cycles of stem **growth, contraction, and
recovery**. The work shows how each type of drought leaves a distinct signature
on stem dynamics, and how trees recover once conditions ease.

This is the first published chapter of my PhD.

👉 **[Feuer et al. (2025), *Plant, Cell & Environment*](https://doi.org/10.1111/pce.15604)**

## Climate coverage of the global tree-ring network

*Where the tree-ring record represents the world's climates — and where climate change is moving beyond it.*

The **International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB)** is the largest archive of
tree-ring records on Earth, and it underpins much of what we know about how
forests respond to climate. But the network was not designed as a climatic
sample: some climates are densely represented, others barely at all.

This project asks how well the ITRDB **covers the range of climates trees
actually experience**, and how that coverage shifts as the climate warms. Two
ideas sit at its core:

- **Space-for-time substitution.** Much of forest ecology assumes that spatial
  climate gradients can stand in for change over time — that a warmer *place*
  tells us about a warmer *future*. I test how far that substitution actually
  holds across the tree-ring network: where places are interchangeable, and
  where they are not.
- **Novel climates.** As warming pushes trees into climatic conditions with no
  analog in the existing record, parts of the world move **outside the sampled
  envelope**. I map where coverage is dense versus sparse, identify the emerging
  novel climates the ITRDB cannot yet speak to, and highlight where new sampling
  would most improve our ability to anticipate forest responses.

The result is a map of both the **reach and the blind spots** of one of ecology's
most important datasets, at a moment when those blind spots are growing.

## A dynamical-systems model of tree mortality

*Treating survival and death as stable states — and asking what tips a tree from one to the other.*

Building on and extending the framework of Trugman and colleagues, this project
models tree survival as a **dynamical system** with more than one stable state.
A tree carrying healthy carbon reserves and intact water-transport tissue sits in
a "living" basin; a tree that is carbon-starved or hydraulically failed sits in a
"mortality" basin. Between them lies a **separatrix** — a threshold that, once
crossed, is hard to come back from.

The model tracks two coupled state variables through time:

- **Nonstructural carbohydrate (NSC) reserves** — the tree's stored energy budget.
- **Xylem / hydraulic integrity** — the functioning of its water-transport system.

**Disturbances** — droughts and heatwaves — reshape this phase space. I
characterize them by their **frequency, duration, and intensity**, and ask how
each dimension bends the system's stable states and pushes a tree toward, or
across, the mortality threshold. Because disturbances arrive in sequence, the
model also captures how **repeated** shocks accumulate: how a tree weakened by
one drought meets the next.

The aim is a deliberately **simple, interpretable** model — one that makes the
mechanisms of resilience and tipping legible, rather than burying them in
complexity.

## Future directions

My longer-term interest is the **mechanistic basis of tree growth and mortality
under climate change** — how the twin currencies of tree health, **carbon** and
**water**, are drawn down by climate extremes, and how that determines which
trees recover and which cross the line into decline.

I want to keep working across scales and methods: from **individual-tree
physiology** measured at high resolution, to **continental patterns** in the
tree-ring record, to **mechanistic models** that tie the two together. The unifying
goal is to forecast forest **resilience and vulnerability** in a warming world —
to understand not just how trees respond to the climate they have known, but how
they will fare in the climates they are about to meet.

I am **seeking postdoc opportunities beginning fall 2027**, and I welcome
conversations about projects and collaborations along these lines.
